stem: Which choice states the belief that the forecaster's request depends on?
stimulus: For decades, a regional weather office has launched weather balloons twice a day to measure temperature and moisture high in the atmosphere. This year, its lead forecaster asked for four launches a day during storm season, when thunderstorms can build within a few hours. The request suggests that, in the forecaster's view, ______
choices: twice-daily launches can miss conditions that change quickly in storm season.
four launches a day would be no more useful than two in storm season.
weather balloons are of no use at all for forecasting thunderstorms.
thunderstorms form far more often now than they did decades ago.
explanation: Ask why anyone would make this request. You only ask for more launches if you think the current two leave gaps, and the passage points to the gap: storms can build within a few hours, so they can form between launches. Choice A states that belief and nothing more. This is the basic move behind every 'What must this person believe?' inference question: when someone asks for more of a tool, they think the current amount falls short.

B.why: You reversed the comparison. The forecaster asked for more launches, which only makes sense if four would do better than two. This choice says the opposite of what the request depends on.

C.why: You pushed 'limited' all the way to 'useless.' The forecaster wants more balloon launches, so the forecaster clearly thinks balloons are useful. The belief is only that two a day is not enough.

D.why: You gave the forecaster a belief the request never needed. The passage says storms build quickly, not that they have become more common. The request makes sense even if storm frequency has not changed at all.

stem: Which choice states the belief that the musicologist's approach depends on?
stimulus: Most orchestras perform Anna Lindqvist's Second Symphony from its printed first edition. When musicologist Pieter Haas prepared a new score, however, he checked every page of that edition against Lindqvist's handwritten draft, noting that music engravers of the period often quietly altered notes they judged to be mistakes. This approach suggests Haas thought that ______
choices: the handwritten draft had itself been copied out from the printed edition.
the symphony is the most important work Lindqvist ever composed.
the printed edition might not match exactly what Lindqvist had written.
every note in the printed edition had been changed by its engravers.
explanation: Why check a printed score against the composer's own handwriting? Because you suspect the printed version may differ from it, and the passage gives the reason: engravers sometimes altered notes. Choice C states that belief, with the cautious 'might' the action calls for. This one-step move unlocks the 'What must this person believe?' questions, where a researcher's choice of source shows what they distrust.

A.why: You reversed the direction. Haas treats the handwritten draft as the original that the printed edition might have drifted from. If the draft were copied from the edition, checking against it would show nothing.

B.why: You picked a belief about the symphony's reputation, not one the method depends on. Haas's checking makes sense however highly he ranks the piece, so this doesn't explain the action.

D.why: You let 'often altered some notes' grow into 'changed every note.' Haas only needs to suspect some changes to justify checking. Watch for 'every' in the choices: it is stronger than anything the action requires.

stem: Which choice states the belief that the linguist's method depends on?
stimulus: Many young adults in the region now study the Veska language in school, and some researchers record these students when documenting it. Linguist Marta Oyelaran, by contrast, recorded only elderly speakers who had learned Veska at home as children. Her choice of speakers suggests that, in her view, ______
choices: students who learned Veska in school speak it more accurately than elderly speakers.
speakers who learned Veska as children may keep features that school learners lack.
young adults who studied Veska in school cannot speak it at all.
Veska will certainly disappear within a single generation.
explanation: Oyelaran deliberately skipped the school learners and chose people who grew up speaking Veska. A reasonable researcher does that only if she thinks the childhood speakers offer something the students don't. Choice B says exactly that, and the 'may' keeps it as modest as the action itself. This unlocks the 'What must this person believe?' questions built on a 'by contrast' choice: picking one group over another shows which group the person trusts more.

A.why: You reversed the comparison. Oyelaran chose the elderly speakers over the students, so she must think the elderly speakers are the better source, not the worse one.

C.why: You turned 'less suited to this project' into 'can't speak it at all.' Leaving the students out only shows she prefers childhood speakers. It doesn't show she thinks the students know nothing.

D.why: You added a belief the method never needed, and made it certain. The passage says nothing about how fast Veska is disappearing, and 'certainly' is far stronger than anything her choice of speakers supports.

stem: Which choice states the belief that the researchers' recommendation depends on?
stimulus: Vaccine studies have long judged a person's protection by measuring antibody levels in the blood. A team of immunologists recently recommended also counting T cells, a separate kind of immune cell, after finding that some volunteers with low antibody levels still resisted infection. The team's recommendation implies that ______
choices: T cell counts are a less complete measure of protection than antibody levels.
the volunteers with low antibody levels had never been exposed to the virus.
antibody levels reveal nothing at all about whether a person is protected.
antibody levels alone may not capture all of a person's protection.
explanation: The team didn't replace antibody testing. They recommended adding a second measure. You add a tool when you think the current one leaves something out, and the volunteers who stayed protected despite low antibodies are the evidence. Choice D states that belief at the right strength: 'alone' and 'may not capture all.' This is the core of the 'What must this person believe?' questions: recommending a new tool shows that the person thinks the current one has a limit.

A.why: You reversed the comparison. The team wants to add T cells because antibodies missed some of the protection. Calling T cells the less complete measure turns their reasoning around.

B.why: You added an extra assumption to explain the result away. The passage gives no sign the volunteers avoided the virus, and the team's recommendation only makes sense if they think something besides antibodies protected these volunteers.

C.why: You turned 'limited' into 'useless.' The team said to count T cells as well as antibodies, so they still value antibody levels. They only think antibodies don't tell the whole story.
